hypothesis: Question: do within-date weather aggregates (whole-day mean/max temp, humidity, wind, worst weathersit, rainy-hour fraction), adjacent-hour weather (previous/next hour conditions), or an explicit hierarchical decomposition (predicted daily total × normalized predicted hour share) represent the rental process better than the flat hourly model that the recorded runs selected? Prior evidence that changed my view: in action 527d5223... and 617ee9b8... the horizon-matched internal folds ranked log1p-target + smearing + calendar/harmonic engineering best (weighted RMSE 93.42; per-fold 103.32 / 75.02), Poisson loss was clearly worse (111.38), recency weighting with 180-day half-life was worse (96.66), and dropping elapsed_day was much worse (mean RMSE 114.05 vs 89.17), i.e. a trend/level feature is needed. Actual development row RMSE for the selected branch was 55.97 with equal-date MAE 36.49, far below internal fold RMSE, so internal folds (March-April dates) are systematically harder than the May-June development window; internal scores are therefore usable only as a ranking signal, not as a level estimate. That gap made me stop tuning the same flat GBM hyperparameters and instead test competing representational assumptions. Contrasting expected outcomes stated before execution: (a) day-level weather context plus adjacent-hour weather improves internal weighted RMSE by >2% relative to the flat replicate, which would mean people's hourly decisions respond to the day's overall and recent weather rather than only the concurrent hour; (b) no improvement or a regression, which would be an informative negative result that the supplied concurrent-hour normalized weather already carries the transferable weather signal; (c) the hierarchical day-total × hour-share model beats both flats, supporting level/shape separation as the transferable structure, or (more likely in my current view) it loses because share normalization forces each date's total onto a single day-level prediction and propagates day-level error to every hour. A 2-of-3-component average is also scored so that an ensemble option can win only if it actually improves the same horizon-matched internal criterion. Transductive use is explicit: day aggregates, neighbour-hour lookups and hour-share normalization use unlabeled evaluation covariates grouped by date; no evaluation labels are used anywhere. The program reports the branch it actually selects, its internal score, the flat replicate score and any fallback use, so a valid vector cannot silently impersonate the intended component.
